```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# ---- Global knitr options: every chunk inherits these -----------------------
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,            # show the code (this is a portfolio: the code IS the evidence)
  message = FALSE,        # hide package start-up chatter
  warning = FALSE,        # hide non-critical warnings (checked during development)
  fig.align = "center",   # centre all figures
  fig.width = 8.5,        # default figure width in inches
  fig.height = 4.8,       # default figure height in inches
  out.width = "100%",     # scale figures to the text width
  dpi = 200,              # print-quality resolution
  comment = "#>"          # prefix for printed output
)

# ---- Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, stringr, forcats, purrr
library(scales)      # percent / dollar axis labels
library(patchwork)   # combine several ggplots into one figure
library(knitr)       # kable tables
library(kableExtra)  # table styling for PDF
library(broom)       # tidy model and test output
library(ggrepel)     # non-overlapping text labels

set.seed(2026)       # makes every bootstrap in this report reproducible

# ---- Load the shared cleaning functions and ALL cleaned datasets ------------
source("R/helpers.R")                 # cleaning functions, palettes, theme
dat <- load_clean_data("data")        # reads and cleans the ten CSV files
crude    <- dat$crude                 # daily Brent / WTI
fuel     <- dat$fuel                  # monthly crude price 1970-2026
country  <- dat$country               # country macro impacts
petrol   <- dat$petrol                # pump prices, four snapshots
petrol_long <- dat$petrol_long        # same, one row per country-date
proscons <- dat$proscons              # pros and cons of the war
timeline <- dat$timeline              # event timeline
voy      <- dat$voy                   # four Hormuz trade-tracker indexes

# ---- Formatting helpers used in the narrative -------------------------------
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ","), "%")
fmt_usd <- function(x, d = 2) paste0("USD ", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ","))
fmt_num <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
fmt_p   <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
fmt_d   <- function(d) format(d, "%d %b %Y")

# A consistent look for every table in the PDF
nice_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, digits = 2, font_size = 8, scale = TRUE) {
  opts <- c("striped", "hold_position")
  if (scale) opts <- c(opts, "scale_down")
  knitr::kable(df, booktabs = TRUE, caption = caption, digits = digits, linesep = "",
               format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = opts, font_size = font_size, position = "center") %>%
    kableExtra::row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
}
```

```{r facts, include=FALSE}
# ---- Headline numbers quoted in the Executive Summary -----------------------
# (Computed here, silently, so the summary can sit at the front of the report.
#  Each number is recomputed with full explanation in the analysis sections.)

# Oil price anchors ------------------------------------------------------------
pre_base    <- mean(crude$Brent_USD[crude$Phase == "Pre-Conflict"])   # pre-war Brent average
peak_i      <- which.max(crude$Brent_USD)                              # row of the highest price
brent_peak  <- crude$Brent_USD[peak_i]
peak_date   <- crude$Date[peak_i]
brent_last  <- crude$Brent_USD[which.max(crude$Date)]                  # latest price (13 Jul)
peak_pct    <- (brent_peak / pre_base - 1) * 100
last_pct    <- (brent_last / pre_base - 1) * 100

# Historical context -----------------------------------------------------------
fuel_mkt    <- fuel %>% filter(!is.na(Log_Ret))
latest_m    <- fuel_mkt %>% filter(Date == max(Date))                  # March 2026
hist_m      <- fuel_mkt %>% filter(Date < max(Date))                   # everything before it
z_mar       <- (latest_m$Log_Ret - mean(hist_m$Log_Ret)) / sd(hist_m$Log_Ret)
n_bigger    <- sum(hist_m$Log_Ret >= latest_m$Log_Ret)

# Pump prices ------------------------------------------------------------------
pump_median <- median(petrol$Pct_Since_War_Calc)
pump_top    <- petrol %>% slice_max(Pct_Since_War_Calc, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
n_full      <- sum(petrol$Pct_Since_War_Calc / last_pct >= 0.8)
n_shield    <- sum(petrol$Pct_Since_War_Calc / last_pct < 0.3)

# Country impacts --------------------------------------------------------------
m_ex_f      <- lm(GDP_Impact_Pct ~ Oil_Import_Pct, data = filter(country, Country != "Iran"))
slope10_f   <- coef(m_ex_f)[["Oil_Import_Pct"]] * 10
pop_hi_f    <- sum(country$Population_M[country$Vulnerability %in% c("High", "Critical")]) /
               sum(country$Population_M) * 100

# Trade tracker ----------------------------------------------------------------
voy_f <- voy %>% group_by(Series) %>%
  summarise(Latest30 = mean(Pct_Baseline[Date > max(Date) - 30]),
            Since_War = mean(Pct_Baseline[Date >= WAR_START]),
            Below50 = min(Date[Date >= WAR_START & MA7_Pct < 50]),
            Days50 = as.numeric(Below50 - WAR_START), .groups = "drop")
vf <- function(s, col) voy_f[[col]][voy_f$Series == s]                 # quick look-up
last_flow_date <- max(voy$Date)
```

\newpage

# Executive Summary

**The story in one paragraph.** On 28 February 2026 a war between the United States, Israel and Iran began, and on 1 March the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil normally flows, was closed. This portfolio joins ten datasets (daily oil prices, 56 years of oil history, pump prices in 14 countries, macro-economic damage in 17 countries, a war timeline, a pros-and-cons ledger, and four ship-traffic indexes) to answer one practical question: **who is paying for the shock, how much, and what should decision-makers do about it?**

**What the evidence says**

* **Oil price shock.** Brent crude rose from a pre-war average of `r fmt_usd(pre_base)` to a peak of `r fmt_usd(brent_peak)` on `r fmt_d(peak_date)` (**+`r fmt_pct(peak_pct)`**) and stood at `r fmt_usd(brent_last)` (**+`r fmt_pct(last_pct)`**) on the last price date. The four conflict phases have clearly different price levels (Kruskal-Wallis test, p < 0.001).
* **Historically extreme.** March 2026 added **`r fmt_pct(latest_m$Pct_Chg)`** to the monthly oil price in a single month: a `r fmt_num(z_mar)`-standard-deviation event. Only `r n_bigger` of the `r nrow(hist_m)` months since 1970 saw a bigger monthly jump.
* **Pain at the pump is uneven and political.** The median pump-price rise across 14 countries is **`r fmt_pct(pump_median)`**, but it ranges from 0% (Iran, Saudi Arabia) to **`r fmt_pct(pump_top$Pct_Since_War_Calc)`** (`r pump_top$Country`). `r n_full` countries passed on at least 80% of the crude price rise to motorists, while `r n_shield` shielded drivers almost entirely through subsidies or administered prices.
* **Import dependence is costly.** Excluding Iran (a war party), every extra 10 percentage points of oil-import dependence is associated with **`r fmt_num(slope10_f, 2)` percentage points** of GDP impact. About **`r fmt_pct(pop_hi_f, 0)`** of the population of the 17 countries studied lives in a country rated High or Critical for vulnerability.
* **Physical trade has collapsed, not just prices.** Against their pre-war normal, crude-oil export traffic through the strait averaged **`r fmt_pct(vf("Crude oil exports", "Latest30"), 1)`** over the 30 days to `r fmt_d(last_flow_date)`, LNG **`r fmt_pct(vf("LNG exports", "Latest30"), 1)`**, fertiliser **`r fmt_pct(vf("Fertiliser exports", "Latest30"), 1)`** and agricultural imports **`r fmt_pct(vf("Agricultural imports", "Latest30"), 1)`**. Crude flows fell below half of normal within **`r vf("Crude oil exports", "Days50")` days** of the war starting; food-related imports took **`r vf("Agricultural imports", "Days50")` days**, a visible domino effect from energy to fertiliser to food.

**Why it matters.** Energy is the first domino; food is the last. Oil-importing developing economies face a triple squeeze: costlier fuel, costlier fertiliser and weaker currencies. The data show that policy choices (subsidies, reserves, diversification) separate countries that absorb the shock from countries that are overwhelmed by it.

**What to do (detail in Section 7).** (1) Governments should target relief rather than freeze prices for everyone, and build 90-day reserves. (2) Importers and businesses should diversify away from Hormuz-dependent supply and hedge fuel and fertiliser costs. (3) Development agencies should prioritise the countries in the most-affected cluster for balance-of-payments and food-security support. (4) Analysts should monitor shipping-flow indexes as a leading indicator, because flows moved days before prices did.

# Business Problem and Questions

## The problem statement

> *A major conflict has disrupted the world's most important oil chokepoint. Decision-makers (finance ministries, central banks, fuel importers, fertiliser buyers, aid agencies and households) need to know: how large is the shock, how does it travel from the oil market to the pump and to the economy, who is most exposed, and which responses appear to work?*

## Who would use this analysis?

| Audience | What they need to decide |
|:--------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Ministries of finance / energy | Subsidy design, reserve release, financing needs |
| Central banks | Inflation and currency-pressure outlook |
| Fuel, fertiliser and food importers | Procurement timing, hedging, alternative routes |
| Development and humanitarian agencies | Which countries to prioritise for support |
| Investors and risk teams | Exposure of markets and sectors to the shock |
| Journalists, students, the public | A clear, evidence-based picture of the crisis |

## Business questions the ten datasets can answer

The questions below were written **after profiling every dataset** (columns, grain, time span, quality). They are phrased in everyday language. The last column shows where this report answers each one; questions marked "Shiny" are best explored interactively in the companion app.

# Data Overview

Ten CSV files were supplied. They fall into three groups that answer different layers of the same story: **price** (what the world paid), **people** (who was hurt) and **ships** (what physically moved).

```{r data-inventory}
# Read every raw file once, exactly as supplied (before any cleaning)
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
raw <- map(files, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)    # one tibble per file
names(raw) <- basename(files)

# Hand-written description of each file (grain = what one row represents)
descr <- tribble(
  ~File, ~Group, ~Grain, ~Period,
  "crude_oil_daily.csv", "Price", "One trading day", "16 Feb - 13 Jul 2026",
  "fuel_prices_1970_2026.csv", "Price", "One month", "Jan 1970 - Mar 2026",
  "petrol_prices_comparison.csv", "Price", "One country, 4 snapshots", "Before war, 7 Mar, 6 Apr, 13 Jul 2026",
  "country_impact.csv", "People", "One country", "2026 war impact",
  "pros_cons_analysis.csv", "People", "One pro or con", "2026 war impact",
  "war_timeline.csv", "People", "One event", "1 Dec 2025 - 13 Jul 2026",
  "crude_oil_export_voy_intake_index.csv", "Ships", "One calendar day", "1 Jan 2025 - 19 Nov 2026",
  "lng_export_voy_intake_index.csv", "Ships", "One calendar day", "1 Jan 2025 - 19 Nov 2026",
  "fertilizer_export_voy_intake_index.csv", "Ships", "One calendar day", "1 Jan 2025 - 19 Nov 2026",
  "agricultural_product_import_voy_intake_index.csv", "Ships", "One calendar day", "1 Jan 2025 - 19 Nov 2026")

# Computed facts about each file: rows, columns and missing cells
inventory <- tibble(File = names(raw),
                    Rows = map_int(raw, nrow),
                    Columns = map_int(raw, ncol),
                    Missing_Cells = map_int(raw, ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  left_join(descr, by = "File") %>%
  select(File, Group, Grain, Period, Rows, Columns, Missing_Cells)

inventory %>% nice_table(caption = "Inventory of the ten supplied datasets", digits = 0, font_size = 7)
```

**How the files relate.** Daily oil prices and the war timeline share a calendar. Pump prices and country impacts share country names (13 countries appear in both). The four trade-tracker files share one structure and one calendar (daily, 2025 to 19 November 2026), so they can be stacked and compared. The trade-tracker files run roughly four months *beyond* the price and timeline files, a fact that shapes what we can and cannot conclude (Section 8).

**What the trade-tracker columns mean.** `voy_intake_index` is a daily index of vessel traffic for the commodity (higher means more ships); `ma_7day` is its 7-day moving average; `prior_year_ma_7day` is the same moving average one year earlier (available only from 1 January 2026).

# Reproducible Data-Cleaning Workflow

All cleaning lives in one file, `R/helpers.R`, which both this report and the Shiny app load. The listing below is the **actual code that ran** (it is pulled straight from the file, so it can never drift out of date).

```{r show-helpers, code = readLines("R/helpers.R"), eval = FALSE}
```

## Cleaning decisions in plain language

1. **Dates arrive in two formats** (`2025-01-01` and `1/1/2025`) *within the same group of files*. A single parser tries both and keeps whichever works.
2. **Blank placeholder rows** at the start of the daily price file (16-20 Feb 2026, no prices) are dropped rather than imputed: there is nothing to impute from.
3. **Daily price changes are recomputed** from prices, and checked against the supplied column (below).
4. **Phases are re-created for the trade-tracker data** from the same calendar breakpoints used in the price file, so all datasets speak the same "phase" language.
5. **"Normal" is defined as the average daily index from 1 January 2025 to 27 February 2026** for each flow. Everything is then expressed as a percentage of normal, which makes four different indexes comparable.
6. **"Medium" and "Moderate" impact labels are merged** in the pros/cons file (they mean the same thing).
7. **Free-text policy descriptions are text-mined** into six yes/no flags (e.g. subsidy, reserve release, demand restraint).

## Quality audit: does the data deserve our trust?

```{r audit-checks}
# ---- Check 1: any missing dates after parsing? -----------------------------
stopifnot(!anyNA(crude$Date), !anyNA(fuel$Date), !anyNA(voy$Date), !anyNA(timeline$Date))

# ---- Check 2: date-format mix in raw trade-tracker files --------------------
voy_raw_names <- unname(VOY_FILES)
fmt_mix <- tibble(File = voy_raw_names,
                  ISO_dates = map_int(voy_raw_names, ~ sum(str_detect(as.character(raw[[.x]]$date), "^\\d{4}-"))),
                  US_dates  = map_int(voy_raw_names, ~ sum(!str_detect(as.character(raw[[.x]]$date), "^\\d{4}-"))))

# ---- Check 3: daily series complete (no skipped calendar days)? -------------
gap_check <- voy %>% group_by(Series) %>%
  summarise(Days = n(), First = min(Date), Last = max(Date),
            Missing_Days = as.integer(max(Date) - min(Date)) + 1L - n(), .groups = "drop")

# ---- Check 4: supplied 7-day average vs our own rolling mean ----------------
roll_check <- voy %>% group_by(Series) %>%
  mutate(Own_MA7 = as.numeric(stats::filter(Index, rep(1/7, 7), sides = 1))) %>%  # trailing 7-day mean
  filter(!is.na(Own_MA7)) %>%                                                      # first 6 days have no full window
  summarise(Max_Abs_Gap = max(abs(Own_MA7 - MA7)), .groups = "drop")

# ---- Check 5: supplied daily % change vs recomputed -------------------------
chg_gap <- max(abs(crude$Brent_Ret_Pct - crude$Brent_Change_Pct_Source), na.rm = TRUE)

# ---- Check 6: supplied pump-price % rise vs recomputed ----------------------
pump_gap <- max(abs(petrol$Pct_Since_War_Calc - petrol$Pct_Since_War))

# ---- Check 7: zero-inflation (days with literally no traffic) before the war
zero_tbl <- voy %>% group_by(Series) %>%
  summarise(Zero_Days_Pre_War_Pct = mean(Is_Zero_Day[Date < WAR_START]) * 100,
            Zero_Days_Since_War_Pct = mean(Is_Zero_Day[Date >= WAR_START]) * 100, .groups = "drop")

# ---- Check 8: join coverage between pump prices and country impacts ---------
only_petrol  <- setdiff(petrol$Country, country$Country)
only_country <- setdiff(country$Country, petrol$Country)

# ---- Check 9: flat (administered) prices early in the 1970-2026 file --------
flat_months <- fuel %>% filter(!is.na(Pct_Chg), Pct_Chg == 0) %>% summarise(n = n(), last = max(Date))
```

```{r audit-print}
fmt_mix %>% nice_table(caption = "Check 2: both date formats appear in the raw trade-tracker files", digits = 0)
gap_check %>% nice_table(caption = "Check 3: calendar completeness of the trade-tracker series", digits = 0)
roll_check %>% nice_table(caption = "Check 4: largest gap between the supplied 7-day average and our own", digits = 3)
zero_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "Check 7: share of days with a zero index (traffic literally nil)", digits = 1)
```

**Audit results in plain language.**

* The two date formats are both present, and parsing left **no missing dates** (Check 1 passed).
* The supplied daily price-change column agrees with our own calculation to within **`r fmt_num(chg_gap, 3)` percentage points**, and the supplied pump-price percentage agrees with ours to within **`r fmt_num(pump_gap, 3)` points**: both are rounding-level differences.
* Every trade-tracker series has **`r sum(gap_check$Missing_Days)` missing calendar days**, and the supplied 7-day averages match our own to within **`r fmt_num(max(roll_check$Max_Abs_Gap), 3)`** index points (rounding).
* Some pre-war days have a zero index, especially for **fertiliser** and **agricultural imports** (table above). So we use *averages and moving averages*, never single days, and we report medians alongside means where it matters.
* **Coverage gaps:** `r paste(only_petrol, collapse = ", ")` appears only in the pump-price file; `r length(only_country)` countries appear only in the country-impact file. Cross-dataset country analysis therefore uses the **`r length(intersect(petrol$Country, country$Country))` countries present in both**.
* **Flat early prices:** `r flat_months$n` months in the 1970-2026 file show exactly 0% change (the 1970s data look administered, not market-set), so volatility figures for early decades are likely understated.

### Do the timeline's headline prices match the daily data?

The timeline quotes Brent prices in its text (for example "Brent crude hits $128.50"). We extract each quoted figure and compare it with the daily price file on the same or most recent trading day.

```{r headline-check}
# Pull the first dollar figure that follows the word "Brent" in each event description
headline <- timeline %>%
  mutate(Quoted_USD = as.numeric(str_match(Description, "Brent[^$]*\\$([0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*)")[, 2])) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Quoted_USD), Date >= min(crude$Date))

# For each event date find the latest trading day on or before it
idx <- findInterval(as.numeric(headline$Date), as.numeric(crude$Date))
headline <- headline %>%
  mutate(Dataset_USD = crude$Brent_USD[idx],
         Gap_USD = Quoted_USD - Dataset_USD) %>%
  select(Date, Event, Quoted_USD, Dataset_USD, Gap_USD)

headline %>% nice_table(caption = "Headline Brent prices in the timeline versus the daily price file")
```

Most quoted figures sit within a few dollars of the daily file. Differences arise because headlines quote intraday highs or weekly averages and some events fall on weekends. The practical lesson: **use the daily file for analysis and the timeline only for context**.

A second claim audit: the pros-and-cons file says Brent is "up 79.8% since pre-war levels". Our calculation from the daily file gives **+`r fmt_pct(last_pct)`** at the last price date and **+`r fmt_pct(peak_pct)`** at the peak. The 79.8% figure is therefore somewhat higher than anything in the daily data (it may use a different pre-war base), and **we do not use it**.

# Analysis

## The oil price shock (Q1-Q6)

### How big was the rise? (Q1)

```{r phase-stats}
# Summary statistics for each conflict phase
phase_stats <- crude %>%
  group_by(Phase) %>%
  summarise(Trading_Days = n(),                              # number of price observations
            Mean_Brent = mean(Brent_USD),                    # average price in the phase
            Median_Brent = median(Brent_USD),                # middle price (robust to spikes)
            Min_Brent = min(Brent_USD),
            Max_Brent = max(Brent_USD),
            Daily_Move_SD = sd(Brent_Ret_Pct, na.rm = TRUE), # typical size of daily % swings
            Mean_vs_PreWar_Pct = (Mean_Brent / pre_base - 1) * 100, # uplift versus pre-war average
            .groups = "drop")

phase_stats %>% nice_table(caption = "Brent crude (USD per barrel) by conflict phase")
```

```{r fig-timeline, fig.cap="Brent and WTI crude, 23 Feb - 13 Jul 2026. Shading shows the four conflict phases; the dashed line is the pre-war Brent average."}
# Phase shading rectangles: one per phase, spanning its first to last trading day
phase_bands <- crude %>% group_by(Phase) %>%
  summarise(xmin = min(Date) - 0.5, xmax = max(Date) + 0.5, .groups = "drop")

# A few key events, placed manually so labels never collide
key_events <- data.frame(
  Date  = as.Date(c("2026-03-02", "2026-04-07", "2026-04-12", "2026-06-03", "2026-06-22")),
  Label = c("Hormuz closed,\noil spikes", "Ceasefire\nannounced", "Talks fail,\nUS blockade",
            "Ceasefire\ncollapses", "Peak\nweek"),
  y     = c(133, 62, 133, 62, 136))

ggplot(crude, aes(Date)) +
  geom_rect(data = phase_bands, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = Phase),
            alpha = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +                          # phase background colours
  geom_hline(yintercept = pre_base, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +  # pre-war level
  geom_line(aes(y = Brent_USD, colour = "Brent"), linewidth = 1.1) +      # Brent line
  geom_line(aes(y = WTI_USD,   colour = "WTI"),   linewidth = 1.1) +      # WTI line
  geom_vline(data = key_events, aes(xintercept = Date), linetype = "dotted", colour = PAL[["navy"]]) +
  geom_label(data = key_events, aes(x = Date, y = y, label = Label), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 2.8, fill = "white") +                                # event call-outs
  scale_fill_manual(values = PHASE_COLS, name = "Phase") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Brent = PAL[["navy"]], WTI = PAL[["coral"]]), name = "Benchmark") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(55, 140)) +
  labs(title = "Oil prices climbed in steps, fell during the truce, then surged again",
       subtitle = "Daily closing price, USD per barrel", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_portfolio() + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

> **In plain English.** Before the war Brent traded around `r fmt_usd(pre_base)`. Within weeks it passed USD 100. The ceasefire pulled it back to the mid-80s, but when the truce collapsed in June it jumped past USD 120 and stayed there. At its highest (`r fmt_usd(brent_peak)`, `r fmt_d(peak_date)`) oil was **`r fmt_pct(peak_pct)` dearer** than before the war.

### Are the phase differences real? (Q2)

A difference in averages could be luck. We test it with the **Kruskal-Wallis test**, which asks "do the prices in all four phases look like draws from the same pool?" We use it instead of ordinary ANOVA because prices are trending (not bell-shaped) and one phase has only five days. If the test is significant, **pairwise Wilcoxon tests** (with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for running several comparisons at once) show which phases differ.

```{r phase-tests}
# Kruskal-Wallis: do prices differ across the four phases?
kw <- kruskal.test(Brent_USD ~ Phase, data = crude)

# Epsilon-squared effect size: share of rank variation explained by phase (0 to 1)
k <- nlevels(crude$Phase); n <- nrow(crude)
eps2 <- unname((kw$statistic - k + 1) / (n - k))

# Pairwise Wilcoxon tests with multiple-comparison correction
pw <- pairwise.wilcox.test(crude$Brent_USD, crude$Phase,
                           p.adjust.method = "BH", exact = FALSE) %>% broom::tidy()

# Typical (Hodges-Lehmann) price gap: blockade phase versus pre-war days, with 95% CI
x_block <- crude$Brent_USD[crude$Phase == "Re-Escalation & Blockade"]
x_pre   <- crude$Brent_USD[crude$Phase == "Pre-Conflict"]
hl <- wilcox.test(x_block, x_pre, conf.int = TRUE, exact = FALSE)
hl_est <- unname(hl$estimate); hl_ci <- hl$conf.int

pw %>% transmute(Comparison = paste(group1, "vs", group2), Adjusted_p = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  nice_table(caption = "Pairwise Wilcoxon tests (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values)")
```

```{r fig-phase-box, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Distribution of daily Brent prices (left) and daily percentage moves (right) by phase."}
# Left panel: price levels by phase
p_level <- ggplot(crude, aes(Phase, Brent_USD, fill = Phase)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.45, colour = NA) +                                 # shape of the distribution
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA) +         # median and quartiles
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.55, size = 1.2) +                    # individual trading days
  scale_fill_manual(values = PHASE_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, 12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Price level", x = NULL, y = "Brent, USD/bbl") + theme_portfolio(10)

# Right panel: size of daily % moves by phase
p_move <- crude %>% filter(!is.na(Brent_Ret_Pct)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Phase, Brent_Ret_Pct, fill = Phase)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.55, size = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = PHASE_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Daily move", x = NULL, y = "Daily change, %") + theme_portfolio(10)

p_level + p_move
```

> **In plain English.** The test says the phases are **not the same** (Kruskal-Wallis p `r fmt_p(kw$p.value)`; phase explains roughly `r fmt_pct(eps2 * 100, 0)` of the variation in price ranks, a very large effect). Comparing the blockade phase with pre-war days, the typical price gap is about **`r fmt_usd(hl_est)` per barrel** (95% confidence interval `r fmt_usd(hl_ci[1])` to `r fmt_usd(hl_ci[2])`). Caution: the pre-war phase has only five usable price days, so the interval is wide.

### Was the market more jumpy during fighting? (Q3)

```{r vol-test}
# Fligner-Killeen test: do daily % moves have equal spread across phases? (robust to outliers)
vol_test <- fligner.test(Brent_Ret_Pct ~ Phase, data = filter(crude, !is.na(Brent_Ret_Pct)))
```

> **In plain English.** Daily swings were largest during active conflict and the blockade, and smallest in the pre-war days and during the ceasefire (see the right-hand panel above and the `Daily_Move_SD` column). But the formal test gives p = `r fmt_p(vol_test$p.value)`, so **we cannot claim the difference in jumpiness is statistically proven** with this few days per phase. The honest conclusion: the *level* of prices changed decisively; the *volatility* change is suggestive only.

### Did the Brent-WTI gap widen? (Q5)

```{r spread}
# Brent minus WTI by phase, tested across phases
spread_tbl <- crude %>% group_by(Phase) %>%
  summarise(Mean_Spread_USD = mean(Spread_USD), Min = min(Spread_USD), Max = max(Spread_USD), .groups = "drop")
spread_kw <- kruskal.test(Spread_USD ~ Phase, data = crude)
spread_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "Brent minus WTI (USD per barrel) by phase")
```

```{r fig-spread, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The gap between international (Brent) and US (WTI) crude prices."}
ggplot(crude, aes(Date, Spread_USD)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = Phase), width = 1) +                                 # one bar per trading day
  scale_fill_manual(values = PHASE_COLS, name = "Phase") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Seaborne crude became pricier than US crude", x = NULL, y = "Brent - WTI, USD/bbl") +
  theme_portfolio() + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

> **In plain English.** The premium of Brent over WTI widened from about `r fmt_usd(spread_tbl$Mean_Spread_USD[1])` before the war to `r fmt_usd(spread_tbl$Mean_Spread_USD[4])` during the blockade (test p = `r fmt_p(spread_kw$p.value)`). Oil that must travel by sea, and through risky waters, costs more than oil produced and sold inland in the US.

### Fall after the ceasefire versus rebound after it collapsed (Q6)

```{r swings}
# Locate the three turning points: wave-1 peak, ceasefire trough, blockade peak
w1  <- crude %>% filter(Phase == "Active Conflict (Wave 1)")
cf  <- crude %>% filter(Phase == "Ceasefire & Negotiations")
re  <- crude %>% filter(Phase == "Re-Escalation & Blockade")
pk1 <- w1 %>% slice_max(Brent_USD, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
tr  <- cf %>% slice_min(Brent_USD, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
pk2 <- re %>% slice_max(Brent_USD, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

swing <- tibble(Move = c("Fall after ceasefire", "Rebound after collapse"),
                From_Date = c(pk1$Date, tr$Date), To_Date = c(tr$Date, pk2$Date),
                From_USD = c(pk1$Brent_USD, tr$Brent_USD), To_USD = c(tr$Brent_USD, pk2$Brent_USD)) %>%
  mutate(Change_Pct = (To_USD / From_USD - 1) * 100,
         Days = as.numeric(To_Date - From_Date),
         Pct_Per_Day = Change_Pct / Days)
swing %>% nice_table(caption = "Size and speed of the two big price swings")
```

> **In plain English.** Oil fell by **`r fmt_pct(abs(swing$Change_Pct[1]))`** over `r swing$Days[1]` days after the ceasefire, then rose **`r fmt_pct(swing$Change_Pct[2])`** over `r swing$Days[2]` days as it collapsed. In per-day terms the fall (`r fmt_pct(abs(swing$Pct_Per_Day[1]), 2)` a day) and rise (`r fmt_pct(swing$Pct_Per_Day[2], 2)` a day) were similar in speed, so **this price series does not show a "rockets and feathers" asymmetry** at the crude level. (The pros-and-cons file raises that effect for *pump* prices, which this dataset cannot test.)

### Which kinds of news moved oil? (Q4)

```{r event-study}
# Match every timeline event to the oil-price move on the same trading day
event_moves <- timeline %>%
  inner_join(crude %>% select(Date, Brent_Move_Pct = Brent_Ret_Pct), by = "Date") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Brent_Move_Pct))

# Average move by news category
event_cat <- event_moves %>% group_by(Category_Primary) %>%
  summarise(Events = n(), Mean_Move_Pct = mean(Brent_Move_Pct),
            Mean_Abs_Move_Pct = mean(abs(Brent_Move_Pct)), .groups = "drop")

# Do the SIGNED moves differ by category? (diplomacy should push down, escalation up)
ev_kw <- kruskal.test(Brent_Move_Pct ~ Category_Primary, data = event_moves)
event_cat %>% nice_table(caption = "Brent's same-day move on days with a timeline event, by news category")
```

```{r fig-events, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="The twelve events with the biggest same-day oil price move."}
top_moves <- event_moves %>%
  slice_max(abs(Brent_Move_Pct), n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(Label = paste0(format(Date, "%d %b"), " - ", str_trunc(Event, 32)),
         Label = fct_reorder(Label, Brent_Move_Pct))                       # order bars by size

ggplot(top_moves, aes(Brent_Move_Pct, Label, colour = Brent_Move_Pct > 0)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = Brent_Move_Pct, yend = Label), linewidth = 1.3) +  # lollipop stick
  geom_point(size = 4) +                                                            # lollipop head
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = PAL[["coral"]], "FALSE" = PAL[["teal"]]),
                      labels = c("TRUE" = "Oil rose", "FALSE" = "Oil fell"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Ceasefire news pushed oil down; escalation pushed it up",
       x = "Brent, same-day change (%)", y = NULL) + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** Events labelled *diplomatic* coincided with oil **falling** on average (`r fmt_pct(event_cat$Mean_Move_Pct[event_cat$Category_Primary == "Diplomatic"], 2)` per event day), while *military* and *economic* events coincided with oil **rising**. The test for a real difference across categories gives p = `r fmt_p(ev_kw$p.value)`. Caveat: these are same-day associations on `r nrow(event_moves)` event days, not proof that the event *caused* the move.

## Historical perspective: 56 years of oil (Q7-Q10)

### How rare is a 36% monthly jump? (Q7, Q8)

```{r hist-tests}
# Standardise March 2026 against every earlier month (z-score) and rank it
hist_m86 <- hist_m %>% filter(Date >= as.Date("1986-01-01"))      # "market-priced" era
z_mar86  <- (latest_m$Log_Ret - mean(hist_m86$Log_Ret)) / sd(hist_m86$Log_Ret)
pctile   <- mean(hist_m$Log_Ret < latest_m$Log_Ret) * 100        # share of months it beats

# The eight biggest monthly increases ever recorded in the file
top_spikes <- fuel_mkt %>% slice_max(Log_Ret, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(Month = format(Date, "%b %Y"))

top_spikes %>% select(Month, Price, Pct_Chg) %>%
  nice_table(caption = "The eight largest one-month increases in crude oil, 1970-2026")
```

```{r fig-history, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Crude oil price, 1970-2026 (log scale, nominal USD). Orange points mark the eight largest monthly jumps; the teal diamond is March 2026."}
spike_pts <- top_spikes %>% mutate(Is_2026 = Date == max(fuel$Date))

ggplot(fuel, aes(Date, Price)) +
  geom_area(fill = PAL[["teal"]], alpha = 0.2) +                           # soft fill under the line
  geom_line(colour = PAL[["navy"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = filter(spike_pts, !Is_2026), colour = PAL[["coral"]], size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = filter(spike_pts, Is_2026), colour = PAL[["teal"]], shape = 18, size = 5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = spike_pts, aes(label = Month), size = 3, colour = PAL[["navy"]],
                  min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.5) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_dollar(), breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "10 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "March 2026 sits among the biggest monthly jumps in 56 years",
       subtitle = "Nominal prices (not adjusted for inflation); log scale so equal percentage moves look equal",
       x = NULL, y = "USD per barrel") + theme_portfolio()
```

```{r fig-hist-dist, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Distribution of every monthly oil price change since 1970. The red line is March 2026."}
ggplot(fuel_mkt, aes(Pct_Chg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, fill = PAL[["teal"]], colour = "white") +    # histogram of monthly % changes
  geom_vline(xintercept = latest_m$Pct_Chg, colour = PAL[["coral"]], linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("label", x = latest_m$Pct_Chg, y = Inf, vjust = 1.4, label = "Mar 2026",
           colour = PAL[["coral"]], fill = "white") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-45, 100)) +                                     # a few extreme 1970s values lie off-chart
  labs(title = "A typical month moves by a few percent; March 2026 moved by a third",
       x = "Monthly change in crude price (%)", y = "Number of months") + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** The oil price rose **`r fmt_pct(latest_m$Pct_Chg)`** in March 2026. That is **`r fmt_num(z_mar)` standard deviations** above a normal month (`r fmt_num(z_mar86)` if we use only the market-priced era since 1986) and beats **`r fmt_pct(pctile, 1)`** of all months on record. Only `r n_bigger` months in 56 years were bigger. *The 2020 entry is a rebound from a pandemic collapse rather than a supply shock, a reminder that a big percentage jump from a low base is not the same as a big dollar shock.*

### Do spikes fade within a year? (Q10)

```{r spike-reversal}
# For every month with a >20% log jump, what happened 12 months later?
spike_tbl <- fuel %>%
  mutate(Price_12m_Later = lead(Price, 12),
         Change_12m_After_Pct = (Price_12m_Later / Price - 1) * 100) %>%
  filter(Log_Ret > 0.2) %>%
  transmute(Month = format(Date, "%b %Y"), Price, Jump_Pct = Pct_Chg, Price_12m_Later, Change_12m_After_Pct)
spike_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "What happened 12 months after a spike of more than 20% in one month (NA = beyond the data)")
```

> **In plain English.** History offers **no reliable "prices always come back" rule**. After the August-September 1990 Gulf War spike, prices fell back sharply within a year; after several other spikes they kept climbing. For planners this means the right response is *flexibility*, not betting on a quick reversal.

### Which decades were the most volatile? (Q9)

```{r fig-decades, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Volatility of monthly oil price changes by decade (the 2020s cover only 2020 to March 2026)."}
decade_tbl <- fuel_mkt %>% group_by(Decade) %>%
  summarise(Mean_Price = mean(Price), Volatility_Pct = sd(Log_Ret) * 100,
            Biggest_Monthly_Jump_Pct = max(Pct_Chg), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(decade_tbl, aes(Decade, Volatility_Pct, fill = Decade)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Volatility_Pct, 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Oil was most volatile in the 1970s and the 2020s",
       x = NULL, y = "Std. deviation of monthly changes (log points x 100)") + theme_portfolio()
decade_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "Decade summary of nominal crude prices", digits = 1)
```

## Pain at the pump (Q11-Q14)

### How much of the oil price rise reached drivers? (Q11, Q12)

We define **pass-through** as the pump-price rise divided by the crude-price rise (`r fmt_pct(last_pct)` between the pre-war average and 13 July). A value of 1 means drivers paid the full increase; near 0 means they were shielded.

```{r pump-passthrough}
# Pass-through ratio and a three-way classification
petrol <- petrol %>%
  mutate(Pass_Through = Pct_Since_War_Calc / last_pct,
         Pass_Class = case_when(Pass_Through >= 0.8 ~ "Near-full pass-through",
                                Pass_Through >= 0.3 ~ "Partial pass-through",
                                TRUE ~ "Shielded / administered"),
         Pass_Class = factor(Pass_Class, levels = c("Near-full pass-through", "Partial pass-through", "Shielded / administered")))

petrol %>% arrange(desc(Pct_Since_War_Calc)) %>%
  select(Country, Region, Before_War_USD, Jul13_USD, Pct_Since_War_Calc, Pass_Through, Pass_Class, Extra_50L_USD) %>%
  nice_table(caption = "Pump price change since the war (local currency) and pass-through of the crude price rise")
```

```{r fig-pump-bar, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Petrol price rise from before the war to 13 July 2026, in local currency, coloured by how much of the crude price rise reached drivers."}
ggplot(petrol, aes(Pct_Since_War_Calc, fct_reorder(Country, Pct_Since_War_Calc), fill = Pass_Class)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Pct_Since_War_Calc), "%")), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = last_pct, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL[["navy"]]) +   # crude oil rise for reference
  annotate("text", x = last_pct, y = 1, label = " Crude oil rise", hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PAL[["navy"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Near-full pass-through" = PAL[["coral"]], "Partial pass-through" = PAL[["gold"]],
                               "Shielded / administered" = PAL[["teal"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Pump prices rose from 0% to over 75% depending on government choices",
       x = "Change in petrol price since before the war (%)", y = NULL) + theme_portfolio()
```

```{r fig-pump-lines, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Petrol price index (before the war = 100) at four dates. Flat lines are subsidised or frozen prices; India and Bangladesh held prices until the last interval."}
last_pts <- petrol_long %>% filter(Stage == "13 Jul")             # end points get a direct label
ggplot(petrol_long, aes(Date, Index, group = Country, colour = Region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(data = last_pts, aes(label = Country), nudge_x = 6, hjust = 0, direction = "y",
                  size = 3, segment.size = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = REGION_COLS) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%d %b", expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.2))) +
  labs(title = "Some prices rose in steps; others were held, then jumped", x = NULL, y = "Index, before war = 100") +
  theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** A driver's fate depended less on the oil market than on the finance ministry. Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal, the UAE and the USA passed on most of the crude rise. **India and Bangladesh froze pump prices for months (index flat at 100 until the July step)** and Iran and Saudi Arabia never moved prices at all. Freezing prices is not free: it shifts the cost into government budgets (see the pros-and-cons ledger on subsidy strain).

### Is import dependence what drives the pump-price rise? (Q13)

```{r pump-dep}
# Do pump-price rises differ across the Low / Medium / High import-dependence groups?
dep_kw <- kruskal.test(Pct_Since_War_Calc ~ Oil_Import_Dep, data = petrol)

# Compare with the numeric import share in the country file (13 shared countries)
pc <- inner_join(petrol, country %>% select(Country, Oil_Import_Pct, GDP_Impact_Pct, Stock_Market_Change, Population_M, Vulnerability),
                 by = "Country")
dep_cor <- cor.test(~ Pct_Since_War_Calc + Oil_Import_Pct, data = pc, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

```{r fig-dep, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Pump-price rise by oil-import dependence group (each dot is a country)."}
ggplot(petrol, aes(Oil_Import_Dep, Pct_Since_War_Calc, fill = Oil_Import_Dep)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.55, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Low = PAL[["green"]], Medium = PAL[["gold"]], High = PAL[["coral"]]), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Import dependence alone does not predict how much pump prices rose",
       x = "Oil-import dependence", y = "Petrol price change (%)") + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** Surprisingly, countries that depend heavily on imported oil did **not** see systematically bigger pump-price rises (Kruskal-Wallis p = `r fmt_p(dep_kw$p.value)`; Spearman rank correlation with the numeric import share = `r fmt_num(unname(dep_cor$estimate), 2)`, p = `r fmt_p(dep_cor$p.value)`). Some of the most import-dependent countries *shielded* consumers while some low-import countries (the USA, the UAE) let prices rise. With only 14 countries the test has little power, but the message stands: **pump prices reflect policy choices at least as much as physical exposure.**

### What does it cost a household? (Q14)

```{r tank-cost}
petrol %>% arrange(desc(Extra_50L_USD)) %>%
  transmute(Country, Extra_Cost_Per_50L_Tank_USD = Extra_50L_USD, Price_Before_USD_L = Before_War_USD, Price_Now_USD_L = Jul13_USD) %>%
  slice_head(n = 8) %>%
  nice_table(caption = "Extra cost of filling a 50-litre tank versus before the war: the eight largest increases")
```

> **In plain English.** Filling a 50-litre tank now costs **`r fmt_usd(max(petrol$Extra_50L_USD), 0)` more** than before the war in the country with the largest absolute increase (`r petrol$Country[which.max(petrol$Extra_50L_USD)]`). Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Nepal face similar extra amounts despite far lower incomes, so the burden relative to earnings is much heavier there (the dataset has no income figures, so we cannot quantify the share).

## National exposure and vulnerability (Q15-Q20)

### Who is most exposed? A transparent stress index (Q15)

The file supplies an expert label (`Vulnerability`) but we do not know how it was built. We construct our own **Stress Index**: standardise five measures (oil-import share, GDP loss, stock-market fall, inflation risk, currency pressure) so each has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, then average them. A positive score means worse than the average country in this sample.

```{r stress-index}
z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))                      # standardise to mean 0, sd 1
country <- country %>%
  mutate(Z_Import = z(Oil_Import_Pct),                     # more import dependence = worse
         Z_GDP    = z(-GDP_Impact_Pct),                    # bigger GDP loss = worse (sign flipped)
         Z_Stock  = z(-Stock_Market_Change),               # bigger market fall = worse
         Z_Infl   = z(Inflation_Score),                    # higher inflation risk = worse
         Z_Curr   = z(Currency_Score),                     # higher currency pressure = worse
         Stress_Index = (Z_Import + Z_GDP + Z_Stock + Z_Infl + Z_Curr) / 5,
         Stress_Rank = rank(-Stress_Index))

# Does our index agree with the supplied expert label?
stress_kw <- kruskal.test(Stress_Index ~ Vulnerability_f, data = country)
```

```{r fig-stress, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Stress Index by country (higher = more exposed). Bar colour is the vulnerability label supplied in the dataset."}
ggplot(country, aes(Stress_Index, fct_reorder(Country, Stress_Index), fill = Vulnerability_f)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = VULN_COLS, name = "Supplied vulnerability label") +
  labs(title = "Iran, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh top the stress ranking",
       subtitle = "Average of five standardised measures", x = "Stress Index", y = NULL) + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** Our independent index ranks **`r country$Country[country$Stress_Rank == 1]`** first, followed by **`r country$Country[country$Stress_Rank == 2]`** and **`r country$Country[country$Stress_Rank == 3]`**. It agrees well with the supplied label: the index differs significantly across label groups (p = `r fmt_p(stress_kw$p.value)`), so the expert labels are not arbitrary. Iran is the most stressed because it is a direct war party (GDP impact of `r country$GDP_Impact_Pct[country$Country == "Iran"]`%), not because it imports oil.

### Does oil-import dependence cost growth? (Q16)

We fit a straight line through GDP impact against import share. Because **Iran is an extreme outlier and a war party** (it imports no oil, yet suffers a 22% GDP hit), we fit the line with and without it and test how much one country changes the answer.

```{r gdp-regression}
d_all <- country                                           # all 17 countries
d_ex  <- country %>% filter(Country != "Iran")             # 16 countries, war party removed

m_all <- lm(GDP_Impact_Pct ~ Oil_Import_Pct, data = d_all) # line through everyone
m_ex  <- lm(GDP_Impact_Pct ~ Oil_Import_Pct, data = d_ex)  # line without Iran

# Tidy the slope of each model (per 10 percentage points of import dependence)
tidy_slope <- function(m, label) {
  td <- broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE) %>% filter(term == "Oil_Import_Pct")
  tibble(Model = label, Countries = nobs(m),
         GDP_Change_per_10pts = td$estimate * 10,
         CI_Low = td$conf.low * 10, CI_High = td$conf.high * 10,
         P_value = td$p.value, R_squared = summary(m)$r.squared)
}
reg_tbl <- bind_rows(tidy_slope(m_all, "All 17 countries"), tidy_slope(m_ex, "Excluding Iran"))

# Bootstrap 95% interval for the slope without Iran (resample countries 2,000 times)
boot_slope <- replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(nrow(d_ex), replace = TRUE)                  # resample rows with replacement
  coef(lm(GDP_Impact_Pct ~ Oil_Import_Pct, data = d_ex[i, ]))[[2]]
})
boot_ci <- unname(quantile(boot_slope, c(0.025, 0.975))) * 10

# Rank correlation (robust to outliers) and influence of the most influential country
sp_all <- cor.test(~ Oil_Import_Pct + GDP_Impact_Pct, data = d_all, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
sp_ex  <- cor.test(~ Oil_Import_Pct + GDP_Impact_Pct, data = d_ex,  method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
cook   <- cooks.distance(m_all)
most_influential <- d_all$Country[which.max(cook)]

reg_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "GDP impact (percentage points) per 10-point increase in oil-import dependence")
```

```{r fig-gdp, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Oil-import dependence versus GDP impact. Solid line: fitted without Iran; dashed: fitted with Iran. Bubble size is population."}
ggplot(country, aes(Oil_Import_Pct, GDP_Impact_Pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  geom_smooth(data = d_ex, method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = PAL[["teal"]], fill = PAL[["teal"]], alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(data = d_all, method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = PAL[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population_M, colour = Region), alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Country), size = 3, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = REGION_COLS) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "More import dependence, deeper GDP loss (once the war party is set aside)",
       x = "Share of oil consumption imported (%)", y = "GDP impact (percentage points)") + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** Without Iran, every extra 10 points of oil-import dependence goes with about **`r fmt_num(abs(reg_tbl$GDP_Change_per_10pts[2]), 2)` points less GDP** (bootstrap 95% interval `r fmt_num(boot_ci[1], 2)` to `r fmt_num(boot_ci[2], 2)`; p = `r fmt_p(reg_tbl$P_value[2])`), and import dependence explains about **`r fmt_pct(reg_tbl$R_squared[2] * 100, 0)`** of the variation in GDP impact. If we leave Iran in, the relationship becomes statistically unclear (rank correlation `r fmt_num(unname(sp_all$estimate), 2)`, p = `r fmt_p(sp_all$p.value)`), because **`r most_influential`** alone drags the line. The sensible reading: Iran's damage is about being bombed, everyone else's is about being an importer.

### Do stock markets and the economy fall together? (Q17)

```{r stock-gdp}
stock_cor <- cor.test(~ GDP_Impact_Pct + Stock_Market_Change, data = country, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

Yes. The rank correlation between GDP impact and stock-market change is **`r fmt_num(unname(stock_cor$estimate), 2)`** (p = `r fmt_p(stock_cor$p.value)`): countries whose economies are expected to shrink most also saw the biggest market falls. Financial markets and the real economy are telling the same story.

### How many people are exposed? (Q18)

```{r fig-pop, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Population living in countries by vulnerability label (17 countries in the dataset)."}
pop_expo <- country %>% group_by(Vulnerability_f) %>%
  summarise(Countries = n(), Population_M = sum(Population_M), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Share_Pct = Population_M / sum(Population_M) * 100)

ggplot(pop_expo, aes(Vulnerability_f, Population_M, fill = Vulnerability_f)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(comma(Population_M), "M\n(", round(Share_Pct), "%)")), vjust = -0.2, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = VULN_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(title = "More than half the people in the sample live in High or Critical countries",
       x = NULL, y = "Population (millions)") + theme_portfolio()
```

### Natural tiers of risk (Q19)

Hierarchical clustering (Ward's method) groups countries whose profiles resemble each other. We ask for four groups and then rank the groups by average Stress Index so that Tier 1 is always the most stressed.

```{r clusters}
# Build the feature matrix (five standardised measures), keep country names as row names
feat <- country %>% select(Oil_Import_Pct, GDP_Impact_Pct, Stock_Market_Change, Inflation_Score, Currency_Score) %>% as.data.frame()
rownames(feat) <- country$Country
feat_s <- scale(feat)                                         # standardise columns

hc <- hclust(dist(feat_s), method = "ward.D2")                # Ward clustering
country$Cluster_Raw <- unname(cutree(hc, k = 4))              # cut tree into 4 groups

# Rank clusters by average stress so labels are meaningful ("Tier 1" = most stressed)
tier_map <- country %>% group_by(Cluster_Raw) %>% summarise(m = mean(Stress_Index), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(m)) %>% mutate(Tier = paste("Tier", row_number()))
country <- country %>% left_join(tier_map %>% select(Cluster_Raw, Tier), by = "Cluster_Raw")

# Principal components to draw the clusters in two dimensions
pca <- prcomp(feat_s)
pc_var <- summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:2] * 100               # % variance explained by PC1, PC2
scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>% mutate(Country = rownames(pca$x)) %>%
  left_join(country %>% select(Country, Tier), by = "Country")

tier_tbl <- country %>% group_by(Tier) %>%
  summarise(Countries = paste(Country, collapse = ", "), N = n(),
            Avg_Import_Pct = mean(Oil_Import_Pct), Avg_GDP_Impact = mean(GDP_Impact_Pct),
            Avg_Stock_Change = mean(Stock_Market_Change), Population_M = sum(Population_M), .groups = "drop")
tier_tbl %>% knitr::kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 1, linesep = "", caption = "Risk tiers discovered by clustering",
                          format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 7.5) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "6cm") %>% kableExtra::row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

```{r fig-pca, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Countries plotted on the first two principal components, coloured by risk tier."}
tier_cols <- c("Tier 1" = "#C62828", "Tier 2" = "#F28C28", "Tier 3" = "#F4B400", "Tier 4" = "#2E933C")
ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = Tier, fill = Tier)) +
  stat_ellipse(geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.12, colour = NA, type = "norm", level = 0.9) +  # soft cluster halos
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Country), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = tier_cols) + scale_fill_manual(values = tier_cols) +
  labs(title = "Four natural tiers of exposure",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_var[1]), "% of variation)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_var[2]), "% of variation)")) +
  theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** The data separate into four groups: Iran alone (the war party), a large block of **import-dependent Asian economies plus Turkey, Egypt, Japan and South Korea**, a middle group of **large, wealthier importers** (China, Germany, the UK, Australia), and **low-import countries** (USA, Saudi Arabia, UAE). The second group (import-dependent, growth-sensitive, currency-pressured) is where relief money does the most good.

### Which policy responses go with smaller damage? (Q20)

The `Policy_Response` text was converted into six yes/no flags (see the cleaning workflow). For each flag we compare the average GDP impact of countries that used the response with those that did not. **Iran is excluded** because its response is wartime rationing, not an economic policy choice.

```{r policy-tbl}
policy_labels <- c(Policy_Subsidy_Support = "Price caps, subsidies or tax cuts",
                   Policy_Reserves = "Strategic reserve release",
                   Policy_Demand_Restraint = "Rationing / demand restraint",
                   Policy_Supply_Diversify = "Supply diversification / more domestic output",
                   Policy_Macro_Finance = "IMF support or rate rises",
                   Policy_Security = "Naval / security measures")
d_pol <- country %>% filter(Country != "Iran")

policy_tbl <- map_dfr(names(policy_labels), function(col) {
  flag <- d_pol[[col]]                                          # TRUE where the country used this response
  tibble(Response = policy_labels[[col]], Countries_Using = sum(flag),
         Mean_GDP_Using = mean(d_pol$GDP_Impact_Pct[flag]),
         Mean_GDP_Not_Using = mean(d_pol$GDP_Impact_Pct[!flag]),
         Mean_Import_Share_Using = mean(d_pol$Oil_Import_Pct[flag]))
}) %>% mutate(Difference_pp = Mean_GDP_Using - Mean_GDP_Not_Using)    # positive = smaller loss for users
policy_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "GDP impact (percentage points) with and without each policy response; Iran excluded")
```

> **In plain English.** Countries that diversified supply or used price supports show **smaller** average GDP losses than those that did not (reserve release shows a modest difference), while countries that rationed fuel or turned to the IMF show **larger** losses (they were already the most import-dependent and cash-strapped, so rationing is a *symptom* of weakness, not its cause). **These are patterns across 16 countries, not proof that a policy works**: wealthy, low-import countries could afford the better policies in the first place. They justify further investigation, not a blanket prescription.

## Winners and losers: the pros-and-cons ledger (Q22)

```{r proscons}
# Weighted balance: Critical = 4, High = 3, Moderate = 2, Low = 1
balance <- proscons %>% group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(Items = n(), Total_Impact_Score = sum(Impact_Score),
            Critical_Items = sum(Impact_Level == "Critical"), .groups = "drop")

# Fisher exact test: are CRITICAL impacts concentrated among the cons?
fisher <- fisher.test(table(proscons$Type, proscons$Impact_Level == "Critical"))

cat_tbl <- proscons %>% count(Category, Type) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  left_join(proscons %>% filter(Impact_Level == "Critical") %>% count(Category, name = "Critical_Items"), by = "Category") %>%
  mutate(Critical_Items = replace_na(Critical_Items, 0))
cat_tbl %>% nice_table(caption = "Number of pros, cons and critical-impact items by category", digits = 0)
```

```{r fig-proscons, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Every pro (right, green) and con (left, red) in the ledger, scored by impact level, grouped by category."}
pc_plot <- proscons %>%
  mutate(Signed_Score = if_else(Type == "Pro", Impact_Score, -Impact_Score),   # cons point left
         Title = fct_reorder(Title, Signed_Score))

ggplot(pc_plot, aes(Signed_Score, Title, fill = Type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["navy"]]) +
  facet_grid(Category ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +             # one panel per category
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Pro = PAL[["green"]], Con = PAL[["coral"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4, labels = abs(-4:4)) +
  labs(title = "The ledger is lopsided: severe harms outweigh modest benefits",
       subtitle = "Impact score: 4 = Critical, 3 = High, 2 = Moderate, 1 = Low", x = "Impact score", y = NULL) +
  theme_portfolio(10) + theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

> **In plain English.** The ledger lists **`r balance$Items[balance$Type == "Con"]` harms and `r balance$Items[balance$Type == "Pro"]` benefits**. Harms score `r balance$Total_Impact_Score[balance$Type == "Con"]` impact points against `r balance$Total_Impact_Score[balance$Type == "Pro"]` for benefits, and **`r balance$Critical_Items[balance$Type == "Con"]` of the harms are rated Critical versus `r balance$Critical_Items[balance$Type == "Pro"]` of the benefits** (Fisher exact test p = `r fmt_p(fisher$p.value)`). The benefits are real (shale producers' windfall, faster EV adoption and renewables) but modest and concentrated in rich economies. The harms land on consumers and developing countries. Caveat: the ledger is an expert compilation with 18 items, not a measurement.

## The Strait of Hormuz trade tracker (Q23-Q29)

Everything below is expressed as a **percentage of normal**, where normal is each flow's average daily index from 1 January 2025 to 27 February 2026.

### How far, and how fast, did trade fall? (Q23, Q24)

```{r voy-summary}
# Key metrics per commodity flow
voy_summary <- voy %>% group_by(Series) %>%
  summarise(Normal_Index = first(Baseline),
            Since_War_Pct_of_Normal = mean(Pct_Baseline[Date >= WAR_START]),          # average since 28 Feb
            Ceasefire_Pct = mean(Pct_Baseline[Phase == "Ceasefire & Negotiations"]),  # during the truce
            Blockade_Pct = mean(Pct_Baseline[Phase == "Re-Escalation & Blockade"]),
            Latest_30d_Pct = mean(Pct_Baseline[Date > max(Date) - 30]),               # latest month of data
            Day_Below_Half = min(Date[Date >= WAR_START & MA7_Pct < 50]),             # first day 7-day average < 50%
            Days_To_Below_Half = as.numeric(Day_Below_Half - WAR_START),
            Lost_Normal_Days = sum(1 - Pct_Baseline[Date >= WAR_START] / 100),        # days of normal trade lost
            .groups = "drop")
voy_summary %>% nice_table(caption = "Trade flows as a percentage of normal, and how fast they fell", digits = 1)
```

```{r fig-voy-lines, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="Smoothed (7-day) traffic as a percentage of normal, with daily values in pale lines. Shaded bands are the conflict phases."}
# Phase bands for the trade-tracker x-axis (everything from the war start onwards)
voy_bands <- voy %>% filter(Series == levels(Series)[1], Phase != "Pre-Conflict") %>%
  group_by(Phase) %>% summarise(xmin = min(Date), xmax = max(Date) + 1, .groups = "drop")

ggplot(voy, aes(Date)) +
  geom_rect(data = voy_bands, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = Phase),
            alpha = 0.16, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Pct_Baseline, colour = Series), alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.4) +   # noisy daily values
  geom_line(aes(y = MA7_Pct, colour = Series), linewidth = 1.1) +                      # smoothed line
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +          # normal = 100
  facet_wrap(~ Series, ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SERIES_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = PHASE_COLS, name = "Phase") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b %y") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 200)) +
  labs(title = "Four commodity flows through Hormuz fell off a cliff in March 2026",
       subtitle = "Percentage of pre-war normal (dashed line = 100)", x = NULL, y = "% of normal") +
  theme_portfolio() + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

```{r fig-heatmap, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Monthly average traffic as a percentage of normal. Red = collapse, green = normal."}
heat <- voy %>% mutate(Month_Start = as.Date(format(Date, "%Y-%m-01"))) %>%
  group_by(Series, Month_Start) %>% summarise(Pct = mean(Pct_Baseline), .groups = "drop")
month_levels <- format(sort(unique(heat$Month_Start)), "%b %y")      # chronological order
heat <- heat %>% mutate(Month = factor(format(Month_Start, "%b %y"), levels = month_levels))

ggplot(heat, aes(Month, fct_rev(Series), fill = Pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Pct)), size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#B2182B", "#F4A582", "#FFFFBF", "#A6D96A", "#1A9850"),
                       limits = c(0, 130), oob = squish, name = "% of normal") +
  labs(title = "Energy flows collapsed within days; food-related flows weakened more slowly",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_portfolio(9) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

> **In plain English.** Compare each commodity with its own normal. Over the most recent 30 days of data (to `r fmt_d(last_flow_date)`), crude oil export traffic is running at **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Latest_30d_Pct[1])`** of normal, LNG at **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Latest_30d_Pct[2])`**, fertiliser at **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Latest_30d_Pct[3])`** and agricultural imports at **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Latest_30d_Pct[4])`**. That is nearly a complete shutdown. Since the war began, the world has lost the equivalent of about **`r fmt_num(voy_summary$Lost_Normal_Days[1], 0)` days** of normal crude-export traffic, **`r fmt_num(voy_summary$Lost_Normal_Days[2], 0)`** of LNG, **`r fmt_num(voy_summary$Lost_Normal_Days[3], 0)`** of fertiliser and **`r fmt_num(voy_summary$Lost_Normal_Days[4], 0)`** of agricultural imports.

### Is the collapse statistically real, and how big is it? (Q23)

For each flow we compare **every pre-war day** with **every day since the war began (28 February)**, using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (suitable for skewed, zero-heavy data) plus a bootstrap interval for the percentage drop in the average.

```{r voy-tests}
voy_tests <- map_dfr(levels(voy$Series), function(s) {
  pre  <- voy$Index[voy$Series == s & voy$Date <  WAR_START]       # all pre-war days
  post <- voy$Index[voy$Series == s & voy$Date >= WAR_START]       # all days since the war began
  wt   <- wilcox.test(pre, post, conf.int = TRUE, exact = FALSE)   # rank-sum test
  auc  <- unname(wt$statistic) / (length(pre) * length(post))      # P(random pre-war day > random post-war day)
  bs   <- replicate(2000, 1 - mean(sample(post, replace = TRUE)) / mean(sample(pre, replace = TRUE)))
  tibble(Series = s, Pre_War_Mean = mean(pre), Since_War_Mean = mean(post),
         Drop_Pct = (1 - mean(post) / mean(pre)) * 100,
         Drop_CI_Low = unname(quantile(bs, 0.025)) * 100, Drop_CI_High = unname(quantile(bs, 0.975)) * 100,
         Wilcoxon_p = wt$p.value, Prob_PreWar_Day_Higher = auc)
})
voy_tests %>% mutate(Wilcoxon_p = fmt_p(Wilcoxon_p)) %>%
  nice_table(caption = "Pre-war versus since-war traffic: size of drop, 95% bootstrap interval and test result", digits = 2)
```

> **In plain English.** The drops are **very large and statistically unambiguous**: `r fmt_pct(min(voy_tests$Drop_Pct), 0)` to `r fmt_pct(max(voy_tests$Drop_Pct), 0)` in average traffic across the four flows, with all tests at p < 0.001. The last column says that a randomly picked pre-war day had more traffic than a randomly picked wartime day with probability between `r fmt_num(min(voy_tests$Prob_PreWar_Day_Higher), 2)` and `r fmt_num(max(voy_tests$Prob_PreWar_Day_Higher), 2)` (1.0 would be certainty).

### Which domino fell first? Did ships move before prices? (Q24, Q27)

```{r dominoes}
# Date each flow first fell below 50% of normal (7-day average)
flow_miles <- voy_summary %>%
  transmute(Milestone = paste(Series, "below half of normal"), Date = Day_Below_Half, Type = "Physical flow")

# Date Brent first rose 10 / 20 / 30 / 50% above its pre-war average
first_cross <- function(th) {
  crude %>% filter(Date >= WAR_START, Brent_USD >= pre_base * (1 + th / 100)) %>%
    summarise(d = min(Date)) %>% pull(d)
}
price_miles <- tibble(Th = c(10, 20, 30, 50)) %>%
  mutate(Milestone = paste0("Brent +", Th, "% vs pre-war"),
         Date = as.Date(map_dbl(Th, ~ as.numeric(first_cross(.x))), origin = "1970-01-01"),
         Type = "Oil price") %>% select(Milestone, Date, Type)

miles <- bind_rows(flow_miles, price_miles) %>%
  mutate(Milestone = fct_reorder(Milestone, Date, .desc = TRUE))          # earliest at the top
miles %>% arrange(Date) %>% nice_table(caption = "Timeline of milestones: physical flows versus oil price")
```

```{r fig-dominoes, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Milestone chart: ship traffic collapsed first; the oil price climbed more gradually afterwards."}
ggplot(miles, aes(y = Milestone, colour = Type)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = WAR_START, xend = Date, yend = Milestone), linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Date), size = 4.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = Date, label = format(Date, "%d %b")), hjust = -0.3, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Physical flow" = PAL[["navy"]], "Oil price" = PAL[["coral"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Ships stopped first, prices followed, food-related trade fell last",
       subtitle = "Date on which each milestone was first reached (war began 28 Feb 2026)", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_portfolio()
```

```{r fig-brent-flow, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Brent price (pre-war = 100) and crude-export traffic (normal = 100) on the same scale."}
cmp <- bind_rows(
  crude %>% transmute(Date, Value = Brent_USD / pre_base * 100, Line = "Brent price (pre-war = 100)"),
  voy %>% filter(Series == "Crude oil exports", Date >= min(crude$Date), Date <= max(crude$Date)) %>%
    transmute(Date, Value = MA7_Pct, Line = "Crude export traffic, 7-day avg (normal = 100)"))

ggplot(cmp, aes(Date, Value, colour = Line)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = WAR_START, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Brent price (pre-war = 100)" = PAL[["coral"]],
                                 "Crude export traffic, 7-day avg (normal = 100)" = PAL[["navy"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(title = "As ship traffic vanished, the oil price climbed", x = NULL, y = "Index") +
  theme_portfolio() + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

# Does the daily price track the daily flow in the days when both are observed?
m_bf <- inner_join(crude %>% select(Date, Brent_USD),
                   voy %>% filter(Series == "Crude oil exports") %>% select(Date, MA7_Pct), by = "Date")
bf_cor <- cor.test(m_bf$Brent_USD, m_bf$MA7_Pct, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

> **In plain English.** Crude-export traffic fell below half of normal about **`r voy_summary$Days_To_Below_Half[1]` days** after the war started; Brent first rose 20% above its pre-war average on **`r fmt_d(price_miles$Date[2])`**. Traffic of LNG and fertiliser fell below half within **`r voy_summary$Days_To_Below_Half[2]`** and **`r voy_summary$Days_To_Below_Half[3]`** days; agricultural imports took **`r voy_summary$Days_To_Below_Half[4]`**. The order (energy, then fertiliser, then food) is exactly the cascade that food-security agencies fear. Interestingly, *day-to-day* the price and the flow are only weakly related (Spearman rank correlation `r fmt_num(unname(bf_cor$estimate), 2)`, p = `r fmt_p(bf_cor$p.value)`): traffic was already near zero for months while the price moved with the news (ceasefire talks pulled it down, escalation pushed it up). **Flows were the first warning; prices then reacted to diplomacy and expectations.**

### Did the ceasefire bring recovery? (Q25)

```{r fig-phase-bars, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Average traffic as a percentage of normal in each phase. Normal = 100."}
phase_voy <- voy %>% group_by(Series, Phase) %>% summarise(Mean_Pct = mean(Pct_Baseline), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(phase_voy, aes(Phase, Mean_Pct, fill = Series)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.85), width = 0.78) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Mean_Pct)), position = position_dodge(0.85), vjust = -0.3, size = 2.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = SERIES_COLS, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, 14)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "The truce brought no real recovery in physical flows",
       x = NULL, y = "Average % of normal") + theme_portfolio(10) + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

> **In plain English.** Even during the April-June ceasefire, traffic stayed at only **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Ceasefire_Pct[1], 0)`** (crude), **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Ceasefire_Pct[2], 0)`** (LNG), **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Ceasefire_Pct[3], 0)`** (fertiliser) and **`r fmt_pct(voy_summary$Ceasefire_Pct[4], 0)`** (agricultural imports) of normal. Prices eased during the truce, but the **physical supply system did not recover**. *Note a data tension:* the timeline states that commercial traffic reached 95% of its pre-war baseline on 16 April, which these tracker indexes do not show. The two measure different things (all vessel traffic versus commodity-specific intake), so we treat the tracker as the better guide to *commodity* flows (see Section 8).

### Where are flows now compared with last year? (Q26)

```{r yoy}
# Latest 30 days versus the same 30 days a year earlier (ratio of sums avoids divide-by-zero)
yoy_latest <- voy %>% filter(!is.na(MA7_PY), Date > max(Date) - 30) %>%
  group_by(Series) %>%
  summarise(Latest_30d_vs_Year_Ago_Pct = sum(MA7) / sum(MA7_PY) * 100, .groups = "drop")
yoy_latest %>% nice_table(caption = "Latest 30 days of traffic as a percentage of the same period a year earlier", digits = 1)
```

```{r fig-yoy, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Latest 30 days of traffic compared with a year earlier (100% = unchanged)."}
ggplot(yoy_latest, aes(Series, Latest_30d_vs_Year_Ago_Pct, fill = Series)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Latest_30d_vs_Year_Ago_Pct), "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = SERIES_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "A year on, traffic is a fraction of last year's level", x = NULL, y = "% of same period last year") +
  theme_portfolio()
```

### Is the food-security chain visible? (Q28)

```{r cor-matrix, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Rank correlation between the four smoothed flow series, before the war (left) and since it began (right)."}
# Correlation matrix of the four 7-day averages for a chosen period, returned in long format
cor_long <- function(d, label) {
  wide <- d %>% select(Date, Series, MA7_Pct) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = Series, values_from = MA7_Pct)
  cm <- cor(wide[, -1], method = "spearman")
  as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) %>% setNames(c("A", "B", "Rho")) %>% mutate(Period = label)
}
cor_df <- bind_rows(cor_long(filter(voy, Date < WAR_START), "Before the war"),
                    cor_long(filter(voy, Date >= WAR_START), "Since the war began")) %>%
  mutate(Period = factor(Period, levels = c("Before the war", "Since the war began")))

ggplot(cor_df, aes(A, B, fill = Rho)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Rho)), size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Period) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL[["coral"]], mid = "white", high = PAL[["teal"]], midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Rank correlation") +
  labs(title = "How closely the four flows move together, before and since the war",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_portfolio(9) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

fert_agri <- cor_df %>% filter(A == "Fertiliser exports", B == "Agricultural imports")
```

> **In plain English.** Before the war, fertiliser and agricultural-import traffic had a rank correlation of only **`r fmt_num(fert_agri$Rho[1], 2)`**; since the war it is **`r fmt_num(fert_agri$Rho[2], 2)`**. A shared shock has tied them together. Caution: after the collapse all four series sit near zero, so a high correlation partly reflects a *common* collapse rather than a causal link from fertiliser to food.

## Putting the datasets together: who is hit by both prices and economics? (Q21)

```{r integrated}
# Link pump-price rises with economic damage for the 13 countries present in both files
int_cor <- cor.test(~ Pct_Since_War_Calc + GDP_Impact_Pct, data = pc, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
```

```{r fig-integrated, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Pump-price rise versus GDP impact for the 13 countries present in both datasets. Bubble size is population."}
ggplot(pc, aes(Pct_Since_War_Calc, GDP_Impact_Pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL[["grey"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population_M, colour = Region), alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Country), size = 3, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = REGION_COLS) + scale_size_area(max_size = 14, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Big pump-price rises and big GDP losses do not line up one-for-one",
       x = "Petrol price change since the war (%)", y = "GDP impact (percentage points)") + theme_portfolio()
```

> **In plain English.** The countries with the largest pump-price jumps are **not** automatically those with the biggest GDP losses (rank correlation `r fmt_num(unname(int_cor$estimate), 2)`, p = `r fmt_p(int_cor$p.value)`). The reason is that government responses re-route the pain: when prices are frozen the damage moves from drivers to budgets, currencies and growth (India, Bangladesh); when prices float, consumers pay first (USA, UAE). **A single indicator, whether pump price or GDP, understates exposure; the combined Stress Index of Section 5.4 is a better guide.**
